topic: Optimal Wordle Strategy: An Algorithmic Approach
target_audience: University students with basic probability/computer science interest

outline.topic: Optimal Wordle Strategy: An Algorithmic Approach
outline.target_audience: University students with basic probability/computer science interest

sections.title: The Game Mechanics: Information Theory Basics
sections.content: Introduce Wordle as a 'Search' problem. Explain that each guess is not just a word, but a query to reduce the search space (the set of remaining possible words).
sections.example: Visual: A large circle (2,315 possible answers) splits into smaller slices based on the feedback of your first guess (e.g., 'CRANE').

sections.title: Prerequisite: Entropy and Information Gain
sections.content: Define Entropy (H) as the measure of uncertainty. An optimal first word is one that provides the maximum expected information (partitions the remaining word set most evenly).
sections.example: Graphical chart: Comparing 'XYZZA' (low info, leaves 500 options) vs 'CRANE' (high info, leaves 60 options on average).

sections.title: The Strategy: Frequency vs. Positional Probability
sections.content: Analyze why letters like E, A, R, I, O, T are statistically superior. We map letter frequency across all 5 slots to calculate a 'Weighted Score' for any candidate word.
sections.example: A heatmap overlay on a QWERTY keyboard showing 'E' glowing bright red, 'Z' in dark blue; a robot character 'WordleBot' calculates a score for 'ARISE'.

sections.title: Algorithmic Walkthrough: The Minimax Algorithm
sections.content: Explain the Minimax strategy: Minimizing the maximum possible number of remaining words after a guess. This guarantees a worst-case performance.
sections.example: A decision tree animation: Root node (guess) branches out into feedback patterns (e.g., G-Y-B-B-B), leading to smaller candidate pools.

sections.title: Practical Application & Summary
sections.content: Conclude with the 'Golden Rule': Use a high-entropy opener (CRANE, SLATE, or ADIEU), then pivot to a 'filter' word if the first guess is ambiguous.
sections.example: A cat character playing the game: It picks 'SLATE', sees a green 'S', and instantly filters its internal database from 2,315 down to 42 options.
